cfa_l2.stem: An analyst estimates ROE = 3.10 + 0.85(Asset turnover) - 1.30(Financial leverage), with both slope coefficients statistically significant. The coefficient on financial leverage is best interpreted as:

options.B: the expected change in ROE for a one-unit increase in financial leverage, holding asset turnover constant.
options.C: the expected change in ROE for a one-unit increase in financial leverage, allowing asset turnover to move with it.
options.A: the proportion of the variation in ROE that is explained by financial leverage.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 34 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. A partial slope coefficient in a multiple regression measures the marginal effect of that independent variable on the dependent variable when every other independent variable is held fixed; the influence of asset turnover has already been removed from it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That describes the simple (one-variable) regression slope, which mixes in the indirect effect running through asset turnover. Multiple regression exists precisely to strip that indirect effect out.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The proportion of variation explained is measured by R-squared for the model as a whole, or by a partial measure; a slope coefficient is a rate of change expressed in the units of the variables, not a proportion.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A multiple regression with three independent variables is estimated on 40 observations. One estimated slope coefficient is 0.64 with a standard error of 0.25. The t-statistic for testing whether that coefficient differs from zero, and the degrees of freedom of the test, are closest to:

options.B: t = 2.56 with 36 degrees of freedom.
options.C: t = 2.56 with 37 degrees of freedom.
options.A: t = 0.39 with 36 degrees of freedom.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 35 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. t = (0.64 - 0)/0.25 = 2.56, and the degrees of freedom are n - (k + 1) = 40 - 4 = 36, because the model estimates three slopes plus an intercept.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 37 comes from subtracting only k = 3 and forgetting that the intercept also consumes a degree of freedom; the correct deduction is k + 1 = 4.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.39 is the standard error divided by the coefficient (0.25/0.64), the ratio inverted. The t-statistic is the coefficient divided by its standard error.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A regression with four independent variables estimated on 44 observations produces a regression sum of squares of 120 and a sum of squared errors (residuals) of 234. The F-statistic for the test that all four slope coefficients jointly equal zero is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 36 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. F = (RSS/k) / (SSE/(n - k - 1)) = (120/4) / (234/39) = 30/6 = 5.00, with 4 and 39 degrees of freedom. The F-test is always one-tailed on the right tail.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.00 comes from dividing the regression sum of squares by k + 1 = 5 rather than by k = 4. The numerator degrees of freedom for the joint test equal the number of slopes being restricted, not the number of parameters.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 3.31 comes from putting the total sum of squares (120 + 234 = 354) in the denominator instead of the sum of squared errors. Only the unexplained variation belongs in the denominator mean square.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: An analyst adds a fourth independent variable to a three-variable regression estimated on 60 observations. R-squared rises from 0.400 to 0.410. The adjusted R-squared of the four-variable model is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 37 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. Adjusted R-squared = 1 - (1 - R-squared) x (n - 1)/(n - k - 1) = 1 - 0.590 x (59/55) = 0.367. The three-variable model's adjusted R-squared was 1 - 0.600 x (59/56) = 0.368, so the new variable raised R-squared but lowered adjusted R-squared - the signature of a regressor whose t-statistic is less than 1 in absolute value.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.378 uses (n - 1)/(n - k) = 59/56, which is the divisor for the three-variable model. Each added regressor costs one more degree of freedom, so the denominator must fall to 55.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.410 is the unadjusted R-squared. R-squared can never fall when a variable is added, which is exactly why it cannot be used to compare models with different numbers of regressors.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A fitted regression gives a predicted value of 8.40 for a particular set of independent-variable values. The standard error of the estimate is 1.20 and the standard error of the forecast is 1.50. Using a two-tailed 5% critical t-value of 2.00, the 95% confidence interval for the predicted value is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 38 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. The interval is Y-hat +/- t x s(f) = 8.40 +/- 2.00(1.50) = 8.40 +/- 3.00. The standard error of the forecast is used because the interval must cover both the uncertainty in the estimated coefficients and the variance of the error term.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 8.40 +/- 2.00(1.20) uses the standard error of the estimate, which reflects only the dispersion of the residuals around the fitted line and ignores the sampling error in the coefficients. The forecast standard error is always the larger of the two.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 8.40 +/- 1.50 applies the standard error of the forecast without multiplying by the critical t-value, which would give roughly a 68% interval rather than a 95% one.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A relevant variable is omitted from a regression, and that omitted variable is correlated with one of the independent variables that was included. The most likely consequence is that:

options.A: the coefficients on the included variables are biased and inconsistent.
options.B: the coefficients remain unbiased, but their standard errors are understated.
options.C: the residuals become heteroskedastic, but the coefficients remain consistent.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 39 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. The omitted variable is absorbed into the error term, so the error term becomes correlated with an included regressor. That violates a core assumption, and the bias does not shrink as the sample grows - the estimates are inconsistent as well as biased. Had the omitted variable been uncorrelated with the included ones, only the intercept would be affected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Unbiased coefficients with unreliable standard errors is the signature of conditional heteroskedasticity or serial correlation, not of omitted variables. Omitting a correlated variable corrupts the point estimates themselves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An omitted variable can leave a visible pattern in the residuals, but the defining and more serious consequence is that the retained coefficients no longer estimate the true partial effects at any sample size.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A researcher estimates one regression of monthly equity returns on the change in the credit spread using 240 monthly observations spanning a long period of administratively fixed interest rates followed by a period of freely floating rates. Pooling the two periods into a single regression is best described as:

options.B: a model misspecification, because the observations are not drawn from a single population.
options.C: an acceptable approach, because a longer sample always lowers the coefficient standard errors.
options.A: a violation of homoskedasticity that robust standard errors would fully correct.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 40 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. Pooling data from two regimes assumes the relationship is stable across them. If the underlying data-generating process changed, the estimated slope is an average of two different parameters and describes neither period. The correct treatment is to test for a structural break and estimate the sub-periods separately.
explanations.C: Incorrect. More observations reduce standard errors only if the added observations come from the same distribution. Adding data from a different regime buys precision around the wrong number.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Pooling regimes often does produce heteroskedastic residuals, but robust standard errors repair only the inference around the estimated coefficient - they cannot repair a coefficient that is not constant over the sample.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: Conditional heteroskedasticity in a cross-sectional regression is best described as:

options.A: error variance systematically related to the independent variables, which makes the standard errors unreliable.
options.B: error variance that changes across the sample but is unrelated to the independent variables, leaving inference largely unaffected.
options.C: error terms that are correlated with one another across observations, which makes the standard errors unreliable.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 41 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. Conditional heteroskedasticity means the variance of the residuals depends on the level of the regressors. The coefficients stay unbiased, but the estimated standard errors are typically too small, inflating the t-statistics and producing too many rejections of the null. The usual remedy is robust (heteroskedasticity-consistent) standard errors, which leave the coefficients unchanged.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That is unconditional heteroskedasticity. It is a genuine phenomenon and the description of its consequences is fair, but it is not the conditional case, which is the one that damages inference.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Correlation of the errors with each other is serial correlation, a separate violation of the assumption that residuals are independent across observations.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A regression with three independent variables is estimated on 100 observations. Regressing the squared residuals on the three independent variables gives an R-squared of 0.14. Using a 5% chi-square critical value of 7.81 with three degrees of freedom, the Breusch-Pagan test statistic and the conclusion are closest to:

options.C: 14.0; conditional heteroskedasticity is present.
options.A: 14.0; conditional heteroskedasticity is not present.
options.B: 0.14; conditional heteroskedasticity is not present.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 42 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.C: Correct. The Breusch-Pagan statistic is n x R-squared from the auxiliary regression of the squared residuals on the independent variables: 100 x 0.14 = 14.0. It is chi-square distributed with k = 3 degrees of freedom and the test is one-tailed on the right tail; 14.0 > 7.81, so the null of no conditional heteroskedasticity is rejected.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The statistic is right, but 14.0 exceeds the critical value of 7.81, so the null is rejected rather than retained. A large test statistic means the regressors explain a meaningful share of the variation in squared residuals.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.14 is the auxiliary R-squared before multiplying by the sample size. The multiplication by n is what turns the goodness of fit into a statistic with a chi-square distribution.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A time-series regression with two independent variables and no lagged dependent variable produces a Durbin-Watson statistic of 1.10. The relevant critical values are d(l) = 1.51 and d(u) = 1.65. The implied residual autocorrelation and the conclusion are closest to:

options.A: 0.45; positive serial correlation is present.
options.B: 0.45; the test is inconclusive.
options.C: 0.90; positive serial correlation is present.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 43 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. For a large sample DW is approximately 2(1 - r), so r is approximately 1 - DW/2 = 1 - 0.55 = 0.45. Because DW = 1.10 is below d(l) = 1.51, the null of no positive serial correlation is rejected. The standard remedy is serial-correlation-consistent (Newey-West) standard errors, which also correct for heteroskedasticity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inconclusive region lies between d(l) and d(u), that is between 1.51 and 1.65. A statistic of 1.10 falls below d(l) and gives a clear rejection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.90 is 2 - DW, which is not the approximation. Positive serial correlation understates the standard errors and overstates the t-statistics, so it does matter which number is used to gauge its severity.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A regression with four independent variables has an F-statistic significant at the 1% level and an R-squared of 0.86, yet none of the four slope coefficients is significant at the 5% level. Regressing the second independent variable on the other three gives an R-squared of 0.90. The variance inflation factor for that variable, and the diagnosis, are closest to:

options.A: 10.0; the regression suffers from multicollinearity.
options.B: 1.11; the regression suffers from multicollinearity.
options.C: 10.0; the regression suffers from conditional heteroskedasticity.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 44 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. VIF(j) = 1/(1 - R-squared(j)) = 1/(1 - 0.90) = 10.0, and a VIF of that size is conventionally read as serious multicollinearity. The classic symptom is exactly the one described: a highly significant F-statistic and high R-squared alongside insignificant t-statistics. Multicollinearity inflates the coefficient standard errors; it does not bias the coefficients themselves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.11 is 1/0.90, using the auxiliary R-squared rather than one minus it. A VIF of 1.11 would indicate almost no overlap between the regressors, which contradicts the symptoms described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The VIF is right, but the diagnosis is not. Conditional heteroskedasticity shows up as residual variance tied to the regressors and is detected with a Breusch-Pagan test; it does not produce the combination of a strong joint test and uniformly weak individual t-statistics.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A first-order autoregressive model for a monthly series is estimated as x(t) = 0.60 + 0.75x(t-1). Assuming the series is covariance stationary, its mean-reverting level is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 45 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. The mean-reverting level of an AR(1) model is b(0)/(1 - b(1)) = 0.60/(1 - 0.75) = 2.40. Above that level the model forecasts a decline and below it an increase, which is what covariance stationarity requires; it exists only because the slope is less than 1 in absolute value.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.80 is b(0)/b(1). Dividing by the slope rather than by one minus the slope gives a number with no interpretation in the model.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.34 is b(0)/(1 + b(1)). The sign in the denominator matters: as the slope approaches 1 the mean-reverting level must rise without limit, and only 1 - b(1) does that.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: An analyst fits an AR(1) model to 100 quarterly observations. The autocorrelation of the residuals at lag 4 is 0.21, with a standard error of 1/(100^0.5). Using a two-tailed 5% critical value of 2.00, the appropriate t-statistic and conclusion are closest to:

options.B: 2.10; the model is misspecified and the fourth lag of the series should be added.
options.C: 2.10; the model is correctly specified, because seasonality cannot affect an AR model.
options.A: 0.21; the model is correctly specified, because the autocorrelation is small.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 46 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. The standard error of a residual autocorrelation is 1/(T^0.5) = 0.10, so t = 0.21/0.10 = 2.10, which exceeds 2.00. A significant autocorrelation at the seasonal lag of quarterly data means the model has left seasonal structure in the residuals; the standard fix is to add x(t-4) as an additional independent variable and re-test. Note that the Durbin-Watson statistic is invalid here, because the regression contains a lagged dependent variable.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The t-statistic is right but the conclusion is not. Seasonality is one of the most common reasons an autoregressive model fails, and it shows up precisely as a significant residual autocorrelation at the seasonal lag.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.21 is the autocorrelation itself, not the test statistic. Whether an autocorrelation is small must be judged against its standard error, which shrinks with the square root of the sample size.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A Dickey-Fuller test on a monthly time series fails to reject the presence of a unit root. Before an autoregressive model can validly be estimated, the analyst should most appropriately:

options.A: model the first differences of the series rather than its levels.
options.B: add a seasonal lag of the dependent variable to the model.
options.C: estimate the model in levels using robust standard errors.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 47 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.A: Correct. A unit root means the series is a random walk (possibly with drift) and is not covariance stationary: it has no finite mean-reverting level and its variance grows with time, so t-statistics from a levels regression are not usable. The first difference of a random walk is the error term itself, which is covariance stationary, and the AR model is estimated on that.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A seasonal lag addresses residual autocorrelation at a seasonal frequency in an already stationary series. It does nothing about a variance that grows without bound.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Robust standard errors repair inference when the error variance is misbehaved in an otherwise valid model. They cannot rescue a regression whose underlying series violates the stationarity requirement.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: An analyst regresses the level of one time series on the level of another, and a unit root cannot be rejected in either series. The t-statistics from that regression can most likely be relied on only if:

options.B: the two series are cointegrated.
options.C: the residuals of the regression also contain a unit root.
options.A: the two series have the same sample mean and variance.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 48 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. Two non-stationary series regressed on each other normally produce a spurious regression - a high R-squared and impressive t-statistics that reflect nothing but shared trending. The exception is cointegration: a long-term economic relationship such that a linear combination of the two series is stationary, in which case the estimated relationship and its standard errors are meaningful.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is the opposite of the requirement. Cointegration is tested by checking whether the regression residuals are stationary; a unit root in the residuals is the evidence that the regression is spurious.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Matching sample moments is neither necessary nor sufficient. A series with a unit root does not have a stable mean or variance to match in the first place.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: The residuals of a time-series model are found to exhibit ARCH(1), estimated as variance(t) = 0.0004 + 0.60 x (error(t-1))^2. The most recent residual is 0.03. The forecast of next period's error variance is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 49 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.C: Correct. Variance = 0.0004 + 0.60(0.03^2) = 0.0004 + 0.60(0.0009) = 0.00094. The practical consequence of ARCH is that the error variance is not constant, so any forecast interval built on a single constant standard error of the estimate is wrong - too narrow after large shocks and too wide after quiet periods.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.0184 uses the residual itself rather than its square. An ARCH model is specified in the squared residual because it forecasts a variance, which must be non-negative.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.00054 is only the second term, omitting the constant 0.0004. The intercept is the baseline variance that persists even after a period with a zero residual.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A researcher fits a model with 45 candidate features to 180 monthly observations. In-sample R-squared is 0.78, but the prediction error on a holdout sample is far larger than the in-sample error. Refitting with LASSO is most likely to help because LASSO:

options.C: adds a penalty proportional to the sum of the absolute coefficient values, shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero.
options.A: adds a penalty proportional to the sum of the squared coefficient values, shrinking all coefficients toward but never to zero.
options.B: replaces the original features with a smaller set of uncorrelated linear combinations of them.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 50 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.C: Correct. The gap between in-sample and holdout error is overfitting: with 45 features and 180 observations the model has partly fitted noise, so variance is high. LASSO's absolute-value penalty performs variable selection by driving weak coefficients to exactly zero, accepting a little bias in exchange for a large reduction in variance and better out-of-sample performance.
explanations.A: Incorrect. That describes ridge regression. Ridge also reduces overfitting, but because it shrinks coefficients without eliminating them it does not produce the sparse, interpretable model that LASSO does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes principal components analysis, an unsupervised dimension-reduction technique. It can also reduce overfitting, but the resulting components are composites rather than a subset of the original features, and PCA never looks at the target variable.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A classifier applied to a test sample of 200 observations produces 40 true positives, 10 false positives, 20 false negatives, and 130 true negatives. Its F1 score is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 51 | Quantitative Methods

explanations.B: Correct. Precision = 40/(40 + 10) = 0.80 and recall = 40/(40 + 20) = 0.667. F1 is their harmonic mean: 2(0.80)(0.667)/(0.80 + 0.667) = 0.73. F1 is the preferred headline metric when the classes are unequal in size, because it ignores the true negatives that dominate the sample here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.85 is accuracy, (40 + 130)/200. Accuracy flatters a classifier on an imbalanced sample: predicting the negative class for every observation would already score 0.70 here without identifying a single positive.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.80 is precision alone, the share of predicted positives that were correct. Precision says nothing about the 20 positives the model missed, which is what recall captures and what F1 combines with precision.

cfa_l2.subject: Quantitative Methods

cfa_l2.stem: A dealer quotes USD/EUR at 1.2000 - 1.2010 and USD/GBP at 1.5000 - 1.5018, where each quote is US dollars per unit of the base currency. A client wishes to buy British pounds and pay for them in euros. The EUR/GBP rate (euros per pound) the dealer will apply is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 52 | Economics

explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.5000 / 1.2010 = 1.2490 is the dealer's bid on EUR/GBP, the rate at which the client could sell pounds for euros. Applying the bid to a client purchase would hand the client the spread, which no dealer does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.5000 / 1.2000 = 1.2500 matches bid with bid. A cross rate must chain the two legs in the direction the transaction actually runs; pairing the same side of both quotes eliminates the dealer's spread entirely.
explanations.A: Correct. The client buys GBP from the dealer at the USD/GBP ask of 1.5018 and funds those dollars by selling euros to the dealer at the USD/EUR bid of 1.2000. Chaining the two ask sides, Ask(EUR/GBP) = Ask(EUR/USD) x Ask(USD/GBP) = (1 / 1.2000) x 1.5018 = 1.2515.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Spot USD/EUR (US dollars per euro) is quoted 1.3000 - 1.3004 and six-month forward points are quoted +26.0 / +34.0, where one point is 0.0001. A corporate treasurer who wishes to sell euros six months forward will transact at a rate closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 53 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.3000 - 0.0026 = 1.2974 subtracts the points. Points are subtracted only when quoted with a negative sign; here they are positive, so the euro trades at a forward premium against the dollar and the points are added to spot.
explanations.A: Correct. The forward bid is the spot bid plus the bid points: 1.3000 + 0.0026 = 1.3026. The treasurer is selling the base currency to the dealer, so the dealer's bid side applies. Note the forward spread of 12 points exceeds the 4-point spot spread, the usual mark-up for the longer horizon and the added counterparty exposure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.3004 + 0.0034 = 1.3038 is the forward ask, the rate at which the dealer sells euros forward. It applies to a treasurer buying euros forward, not selling them.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: The spot rate is USD/EUR 1.2000 (US dollars per euro). One-year risk-free rates are 5.00% in the United States and 1.00% in the euro area, both annually compounded. Under covered interest rate parity, the one-year forward rate is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 54 | Economics

explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.2000 x (1.01 / 1.05) = 1.1543 inverts the ratio, putting the base-currency rate in the numerator. That would place the low-yielding euro at a forward discount, the opposite of what parity requires.
explanations.C: Correct. With the rate quoted as price currency per base currency, F = S x (1 + i_price) / (1 + i_base) = 1.2000 x (1.05 / 1.01) = 1.2475. The lower-interest-rate currency, the euro, must trade at a forward premium so that a hedged investor earns the same return in either currency.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 1.2000 x 1.04 = 1.2480 applies the 4 percentage point differential as a simple add-on. Parity is a ratio of the two gross returns, not a difference applied to spot, and the shortcut overstates the premium here.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: The spot rate is USD/EUR 1.2000, the one-year US rate is 5.00%, and the one-year euro rate is 1.00%, so the parity one-year forward rate is USD/EUR 1.2475. A dealer is quoting the one-year forward at USD/EUR 1.2600. The arbitrage that will restore parity is best described as:

options.A: borrowing euros, investing in dollars, and buying euros forward.
options.B: borrowing dollars, investing in euros, and selling euros forward.
options.C: borrowing dollars, investing in euros, and buying euros forward.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 55 | Economics

explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the trade that profits when the quoted forward sits below parity, that is, when the euro is too cheap forward. Here the euro is too expensive forward, so borrowing euros and buying them back forward locks in a loss.
explanations.B: Correct. The quoted forward of 1.2600 exceeds the parity forward of 1.2475, so the euro is overpriced forward and must be sold. Borrow USD 1.2000 and repay 1.2000 x 1.05 = USD 1.2600; convert to EUR 1.0000, invest at 1% to reach EUR 1.0100, and deliver into the forward at 1.2600 for USD 1.2726. The riskless gain is USD 0.0126 on zero net capital.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Buying euros forward while already long euros through the deposit doubles the currency exposure instead of covering it. The position becomes an outright bet on the euro rather than an arbitrage, and it sits on the wrong side of the mispricing.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: An investor borrows Japanese yen at 0.50% for one year and invests the proceeds in Australian dollars at 5.50% for one year. The spot rate at inception is JPY/AUD 80.00 (yen per Australian dollar) and the rate one year later is JPY/AUD 78.00. Measured in yen on the amount initially converted, the all-in return on the carry trade is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 56 | Economics

explanations.A: Correct. Borrowing JPY 80.00 requires repaying 80.00 x 1.005 = JPY 80.40. The AUD 1.00 purchased grows to AUD 1.055, worth 1.055 x 78.00 = JPY 82.29 at the closing rate. The profit of JPY 1.89 on JPY 80.00 is 2.36%: the 5.00% interest pick-up eroded by the roughly 2.5% depreciation of the investment currency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5.50% - 0.50% = 5.00% is the interest differential alone. That is the carry trade's return only if the exchange rate is unchanged, which is exactly the outcome uncovered interest rate parity says should not persist.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5.00% + 2.50% = 7.50% adds the currency move instead of subtracting it. The Australian dollar fell from 80.00 to 78.00 yen, so the investment currency depreciated and the move worked against the position.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: The historical distribution of returns to the currency carry trade is best described as:

options.B: approximately normal, centred on the interest rate differential.
options.C: positively skewed with fat tails, reflecting occasional large gains.
options.A: negatively skewed with fat tails, reflecting occasional large losses.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 57 | Economics

explanations.B: Incorrect. Carry returns are demonstrably non-normal. Under normality the standard deviation would be a sufficient risk measure, and long calm stretches followed by abrupt reversals would be as likely in one direction as the other, which is not what is observed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is the mirror image of the actual pattern and describes a long option position. The carry trade behaves like a short option: many small gains punctuated by rare large losses, not the reverse.
explanations.A: Correct. The trade collects the interest differential steadily while positions crowd, then unwinds violently when funding conditions tighten and the funding currency appreciates. This crash risk makes returns negatively skewed and leptokurtic, so standard deviation materially understates the true risk.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Compared with covered interest rate parity, uncovered interest rate parity is best described as:

options.C: enforced by riskless arbitrage, so that it holds at every point in time.
options.A: an expectational condition with no enforcing arbitrage, so it fails in the short run.
options.B: a relationship that holds well over short horizons and breaks down over long horizons.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 58 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes covered parity, which uses a forward contract to lock in the future rate and is therefore enforceable by a riskless trade. Uncovered parity leaves the future spot rate unhedged, so a deviation is a risky bet rather than an arbitrage.
explanations.A: Correct. Uncovered parity holds that the expected spot change offsets the interest differential, which requires investors to be risk neutral. Because no trade forces it, it has almost no short-run explanatory power: high-yield currencies have on average not depreciated as predicted, which is precisely what makes the carry trade profitable.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The evidence runs the other way. Uncovered parity describes short-horizon movements poorly but finds more support over long horizons, where it tends to align with the purchasing power parity path.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Expected inflation over the coming year is 6.0% in Country A and 2.0% in Country B. The current spot rate is 5.0000 units of A's currency per unit of B's currency. Under the ex-ante form of relative purchasing power parity, the expected spot rate in one year is closest to:

options.C: 4.8113 A per B.
options.A: 5.1961 A per B.
options.B: 5.3000 A per B.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 59 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. 5.0000 x (1.02 / 1.06) = 4.8113 inverts the inflation ratio and has A's currency appreciating. The higher-inflation currency must lose purchasing power, so more of it, not less, should be required per unit of B's currency.
explanations.A: Correct. With A as the price currency, E(S1) = S0 x (1 + inflation_A) / (1 + inflation_B) = 5.0000 x (1.06 / 1.02) = 5.1961. Relative PPP has the nominal rate move to offset the inflation differential, implying A's currency depreciates by roughly 3.9% over the year.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5.0000 x 1.06 = 5.3000 applies only Country A's inflation. Relative PPP works on the differential, so ignoring Country B's 2.0% inflation overstates the required depreciation of A's currency.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: If the international Fisher effect holds and real interest rates are equal across two markets, the nominal interest rate differential between them is best described as an estimate of the:

options.C: expected inflation differential between the two countries.
options.A: expected change in the real exchange rate between the currencies.
options.B: country risk premium foreign investors require to hold the currency.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 60 | Economics

explanations.C: Correct. The Fisher relation splits each nominal rate into a real rate plus expected inflation. If the real rate is common to both markets it cancels, leaving the nominal spread as the expected inflation spread. Combining this with ex-ante relative PPP produces the uncovered interest rate parity condition.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Under these assumptions the real exchange rate is expected to be unchanged, not to move with the nominal spread. Real exchange rate changes are precisely the deviations that occur when PPP and the international Fisher effect fail to hold.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A country risk premium is one reason real rates differ across markets, so invoking it contradicts the stated assumption that real rates are equal. It would be an extra wedge on top of the inflation differential, not the differential itself.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Under the Mundell-Fleming model with a floating exchange rate and high capital mobility, a government that adopts expansionary fiscal policy while its central bank tightens monetary policy will most likely see the domestic currency:

options.C: appreciate, as both policies push domestic interest rates up and draw capital in.
options.A: depreciate, as the fiscal expansion raises imports and widens the trade deficit.
options.B: remain broadly unchanged, as the two policies offset each other's rate effects.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 61 | Economics

explanations.C: Correct. With high capital mobility the interest rate channel dominates. Fiscal expansion raises domestic real rates through increased government borrowing, and monetary tightening raises them again; the resulting capital inflow bids the currency up. The two policies reinforce rather than offset each other here.
explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the outcome under low capital mobility, where trade flows rather than capital flows set the currency and a fiscal expansion weakens it by pulling in imports. With high mobility the capital inflow swamps the trade effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The policies do not cancel. Expansionary fiscal policy and restrictive monetary policy both push interest rates up. It is the expansionary-fiscal plus expansionary-monetary combination that leaves the rate effect, and therefore the currency, indeterminate.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Which of the following is most likely a warning sign that a country is heading into a currency crisis?

options.C: Official foreign exchange reserves rising relative to short-term external debt.
options.A: Broad money growth slowing sharply relative to nominal GDP growth.
options.B: A real exchange rate well above its historical mean alongside a widening current account deficit.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 62 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. Rising reserve cover is a sign of strengthening. The documented warning sign is the opposite: reserves falling sharply, often because the central bank is spending them defending a peg, which leaves less ammunition and invites a speculative attack.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The warning sign is rapid money growth relative to output, which accompanies rising inflation and an eroding real value of the currency. Money growth decelerating relative to nominal GDP points the other way.
explanations.B: Correct. Studies of past episodes find that a real currency value substantially above its historical mean, signalling overvaluation, together with a deteriorating current account, is among the more reliable precursors. Worsening terms of trade, a prior equity boom and bust, and a preceding banking crisis are the other common markers.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: An economy's output follows a Cobb-Douglas production function with a capital elasticity of 0.30. Over the past year the capital stock grew 6.0%, the labour input grew 2.0%, and total factor productivity grew 1.0%. Using growth accounting, the growth rate of output over the year is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 63 | Economics

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.30(6.0%) + 0.70(2.0%) = 3.2% counts only the measured factor inputs and drops the 1.0% TFP growth. Total factor productivity enters the growth accounting equation as a separate residual term, not through the input weights.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth accounting gives output growth as TFP growth plus the share-weighted growth of each input: 1.0% + 0.30(6.0%) + 0.70(2.0%) = 1.0% + 1.8% + 1.4% = 4.2%. Under constant returns to scale the elasticities equal the factor income shares and sum to one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.0% + 0.70(6.0%) + 0.30(2.0%) = 5.8% swaps the elasticities, applying labour's share to capital. The 0.30 given is capital's elasticity, so labour's is its complement, 0.70.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: An economy with an already high capital-to-labour ratio raises its investment rate but adopts no new technology. Its output per worker is most likely to:

options.B: rise at a constant rate for as long as the higher investment continues.
options.C: rise by progressively smaller amounts as the capital stock accumulates.
options.A: rise because the per-worker production function shifts upward.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 64 | Economics

explanations.B: Incorrect. Constant growth from capital accumulation alone requires capital to escape diminishing returns, which is the endogenous growth assumption, not the neoclassical one. In the setting described, each successive unit of capital per worker adds less output than the one before.
explanations.C: Correct. Capital deepening moves the economy along a fixed per-worker production function into a region of lower marginal product of capital. Output per worker still rises, but by shrinking increments, and growth from this source stops once the marginal product falls to the level that merely justifies replacing depreciated capital.
explanations.A: Incorrect. An upward shift of the entire per-worker production function is what technological progress does, raising output at every capital-to-labour ratio. Capital deepening is a movement along the existing curve, not a shift of it.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: In the neoclassical growth model, an economy has total factor productivity growth of 1.5% per year, a capital elasticity of output of 0.25, and labour force growth of 1.0% per year. In the steady state, the growth rate of output per capita is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 65 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.5% is the raw rate of technological progress. It understates steady-state per-capita growth because it ignores the induced capital deepening: faster productivity growth lifts the marginal product of capital, which attracts additional investment and amplifies the effect.
explanations.A: Correct. Steady-state growth in output per capita equals TFP growth divided by labour's elasticity: 1.5% / (1 - 0.25) = 2.0%. Total output then grows at 2.0% + 1.0% = 3.0%. In the steady state the marginal product of capital is constant, so the real interest rate and the factor shares are constant as well.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.5% / 0.25 = 6.0% divides by capital's elasticity rather than labour's. The correct denominator is one minus the capital elasticity, which is labour's share of output.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: A key implication of endogenous growth theory that distinguishes it from the neoclassical model is that a permanent increase in the saving and investment rate:

options.C: permanently raises the growth rate of output per capita.
options.A: permanently raises the level, but not the growth rate, of output per capita.
options.B: raises growth only until the marginal product of capital has declined.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 66 | Economics

explanations.C: Correct. Endogenous growth models treat knowledge and R&D as capital that spills over to other firms, so capital broadly defined need not face diminishing returns. Growth is then determined inside the model, and policies that raise investment, subsidise R&D, or protect intellectual property lift the long-run growth rate rather than only the income level.
explanations.A: Incorrect. This is the neoclassical conclusion. There, diminishing returns mean a higher saving rate carries the economy to a higher steady-state capital-to-labour ratio and a higher income level, after which growth reverts to the exogenous rate of technological progress.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This restates the neoclassical transition path rather than the endogenous growth result. It is also the mechanism behind the neoclassical prediction of conditional convergence, whereas endogenous growth models predict no automatic catch-up by poorer countries.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: A regulator requires factories along a river to treat their effluent because untreated discharge degrades water quality for downstream users who receive no compensation. The economic rationale for this regulation is best described as addressing:

options.C: an informational friction between the factories and downstream users.
options.A: a negative externality that the market price does not capture.
options.B: the under-provision of a public good by private firms.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 67 | Economics

explanations.C: Incorrect. Informational frictions arise when one party to a transaction knows materially more than the other, the case for disclosure rules and insider trading prohibitions. Here the downstream users are not parties to the factories' transactions at all, and their problem is the cost imposed on them rather than what they know.
explanations.A: Correct. The factory's private cost excludes the damage borne by third parties, so the market price is too low and output too high. Private bargaining could in principle internalise the cost, but with many diffuse affected parties the transaction costs make that impractical, which is the standard case for regulatory intervention.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A public good is non-rival and non-excludable and is under-supplied because free riding makes private provision unprofitable. The problem here is over-supply of a harmful by-product, not under-supply of a beneficial good.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: A bank restructures a transaction so that it is booked through a subsidiary in a jurisdiction with lighter capital requirements, leaving the economic substance of the transaction unchanged. This behaviour is best described as:

options.B: regulatory capture.
options.C: regulatory competition.
options.A: regulatory arbitrage.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 68 | Economics

explanations.B: Incorrect. Regulatory capture is the tendency of a regulator to come to serve the interests of the industry it supervises rather than the public, typically through staff movement and dependence on industry information. It describes the regulator's conduct, not a regulated firm's booking decision.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Regulatory competition is what jurisdictions do when they set lighter or more accommodating regimes to attract business. It is the supply-side condition that makes this bank's trade available, but the bank's act of exploiting the gap is something distinct.
explanations.A: Correct. Regulatory arbitrage captures the difference between two regulatory regimes, or between a rule's letter and its intent, without changing the underlying economics. Because it relocates risk to where oversight is weakest rather than reducing it, analysts treat it as a signal that reported capital ratios understate risk.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: In assessing the likely impact of a proposed regulation on the companies it will cover, an analyst should most appropriately estimate the:

options.A: direct budgetary cost to the regulator of supervising the new rule.
options.B: private compliance costs of the rule less the private benefits it confers.
options.C: public policy objective the rule is formally intended to achieve.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 69 | Economics

explanations.A: Incorrect. The regulator's supervisory budget is a cost to the state, not to the regulated companies, and it is typically small next to what compliance costs the industry. It says little about the earnings or competitive position of the firms being valued.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the net regulatory burden, the measure that reaches company cash flows. A sound assessment also weighs indirect and unintended consequences, which are often larger than the direct costs and hard to estimate before a rule takes effect, which is why sunset clauses forcing reassessment are useful.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The stated objective describes intent, not economic effect. Regulations frequently fail to achieve their stated aims, or achieve them at a cost exceeding the benefit, so the objective cannot substitute for a cost-benefit estimate.

cfa_l2.subject: Economics

cfa_l2.stem: Company P holds none of the voting equity of a special purpose entity, but P designed the entity, directs the activities that most significantly affect its returns, and is exposed to the majority of its variable returns. Under IFRS, P should most likely:

options.C: consolidate the entity, because control rather than an ownership percentage drives the classification.
options.A: apply the equity method, because directing the entity's activities conveys significant influence only.
options.B: leave the entity unconsolidated and disclose the relationship, because P holds no voting shares.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 70 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Correct. IFRS 10 defines control as power over the relevant activities, exposure to variable returns, and the ability to use that power to affect those returns; all three are present here, and no voting stake is required. Consolidation of structured entities on this basis is what removed the older off-balance-sheet SPE technique.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The equity method applies to significant influence, meaning participation in policy decisions without control. Directing the activities that most affect returns is control, which requires consolidation rather than one-line treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A voting-interest test alone was the pre-IFRS 10 weakness that let sponsors keep leveraged SPEs off the balance sheet. Disclosure is not a substitute for consolidation once the control criteria are met.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A company holds a portfolio of corporate bonds whose contractual terms give rise to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest, and whose business model is achieved both by collecting those contractual cash flows and by selling the bonds. Under IFRS 9, the bonds are most likely measured at:

options.A: amortised cost, with unrealised fair value changes disclosed but not recognised.
options.B: fair value through other comprehensive income, with interest income still recognised in profit or loss.
options.C: fair value through profit or loss, with every fair value change recognised in profit or loss.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 71 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amortised cost requires a business model of holding the asset solely to collect contractual cash flows. Selling is integral to this model, so amortised cost is unavailable even though the cash flow test is met.
explanations.B: Correct. IFRS 9 classifies debt instruments on two tests: the contractual cash flow characteristics test, met here, and the business model test. A hold-to-collect-and-sell model gives FVOCI, under which interest income, expected credit losses and foreign exchange still run through profit or loss and only the residual fair value movement sits in OCI, recycled on derecognition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. FVPL is the residual category, used when the cash flow test fails, when the business model is trading, or when the fair value option is elected. Here both IFRS 9 tests point to FVOCI instead.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Under IFRS 9, a company irrevocably elects at initial recognition to present fair value changes on a non-trading equity investment in other comprehensive income. When that investment is later sold at a gain, the cumulative amount sitting in OCI is most likely:

options.B: reclassified out of OCI into profit or loss as a realised gain of the period.
options.C: left within equity, with no amount ever recycled through profit or loss.
options.A: offset against the carrying amount of the investment, leaving total equity unchanged.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 72 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.B: Incorrect. Recycling on disposal is the treatment for debt instruments measured at FVOCI, not for equity instruments under the OCI election. Treating the two alike overstates the net income of a company that harvests appreciated equity stakes.
explanations.C: Correct. The FVOCI election for equity instruments carries no recycling: the cumulative gain may be transferred within equity to retained earnings but never passes through profit or loss, so a disposal gain is invisible in reported net income. The election is also irrevocable, and IFRS 9 permits reclassification between categories only for debt instruments, and only when the business model itself changes.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The carrying amount is already fair value, so derecognition removes it against the sale proceeds; there is no separate offset, and equity is unaffected only because the gain was recognised in OCI in earlier periods.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Under the IFRS 9 expected credit loss model, the loss allowance on a corporate bond measured at amortised cost is most likely first recognised:

options.A: when objective evidence exists that a loss event affecting the issuer has occurred.
options.B: at initial recognition, measured at the losses expected from defaults possible within 12 months.
options.C: when credit risk has increased significantly since purchase, measured at lifetime expected losses.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 73 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Waiting for objective evidence of a loss event is the incurred loss model of IAS 39, which IFRS 9 replaced precisely because it recognised credit losses too little and too late.
explanations.B: Correct. The expected credit loss model is forward-looking: a day-one allowance equal to 12-month expected credit losses is recognised even on a performing, newly purchased instrument. This deliberately front-loads provisioning relative to the model it replaced, so reported income absorbs credit cost earlier in the cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A significant increase in credit risk moves the instrument from 12-month to lifetime expected losses. That changes the measurement of an allowance that already exists rather than creating the first one.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: On 1 January an investor pays EUR 4,500,000 for a 30% interest in an associate whose identifiable net assets have a book value of EUR 12,000,000. The only asset carried below fair value is plant, undervalued by EUR 2,000,000 with a 10-year remaining life; the rest of the excess is goodwill. During the year the associate reports net income of EUR 1,500,000 and pays dividends of EUR 500,000. The carrying amount of the investment at 31 December is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 74 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Correct. The investor's share of book value is EUR 3,600,000, so the excess is EUR 900,000, of which 30% of EUR 2,000,000 equals EUR 600,000 attributable to plant and EUR 300,000 is goodwill. Amortising the plant excess over ten years costs EUR 60,000, giving equity income of EUR 450,000 less EUR 60,000 equals EUR 390,000, so the balance rolls forward to EUR 4,500,000 plus EUR 390,000 less EUR 150,000 of dividends.
explanations.A: Incorrect. EUR 4,800,000 takes the full EUR 450,000 share of net income and omits the EUR 60,000 amortisation of the excess price allocated to plant, the most common equity-method error and one that overstates earnings every year of the asset's life.
explanations.B: Incorrect. EUR 4,890,000 amortises the excess correctly but forgets that dividends are a return of the investment rather than income; the EUR 150,000 received reduces the carrying amount instead of being recognised in profit or loss.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A company applies the equity method to a 30% associate. Part of the excess of the purchase price over its share of the fair value of the associate's identifiable net assets is goodwill. Under IFRS, that goodwill is most likely:

options.C: tested for impairment annually at the level of the associate's cash-generating unit.
options.A: presented as a separate intangible asset on the investor's balance sheet.
options.B: not tested separately, because the whole investment is tested as a single asset.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 75 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Incorrect. Annual cash-generating-unit testing is the regime for goodwill recognised in a business combination and carried on the consolidated balance sheet, not for goodwill buried inside an equity-method investment.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Nothing about the associate is presented line by line under the equity method, neither its assets nor the implicit goodwill. Only the single investment balance appears, which is why the method is called one-line consolidation.
explanations.B: Correct. Equity-method goodwill is embedded in the one-line investment balance and is never identified or tested on its own. The entire carrying amount of the investment is instead compared with its recoverable amount as a single asset when impairment indicators exist, which also means such an impairment may be reversed later, unlike consolidation goodwill.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: An investor owns 25% of an associate and applies the equity method. During the year the associate sold inventory to the investor for USD 800,000; the inventory had cost the associate USD 600,000, and at year-end the investor still holds 40% of it unsold. The associate reports net income of USD 2,000,000. The investor's equity income for the year is closest to:
cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 76 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 450,000 eliminates 25% of the entire USD 200,000 profit. The 60% of the goods already resold to outside parties has been confirmed by a third-party transaction, so that profit is realised and stays in income.
explanations.B: Correct. The sale is upstream, so the profit sits in the associate's reported income. Of the USD 200,000 gross profit, 40%, or USD 80,000, is unrealised because the goods remain in the investor's inventory, and the investor eliminates its 25% share, USD 20,000, from USD 500,000. Under the equity method the same proportionate elimination applies whether the sale is upstream or downstream.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 500,000 is the unadjusted 25% share of reported net income. Ignoring unrealised profit would let an associate inflate the investor's earnings simply by shipping goods that have not left the group.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Under IFRS, an interest in a joint venture is accounted for using the equity method rather than proportionate consolidation most likely because the venturer:

options.B: has rights to the net assets of the arrangement rather than to its individual assets and liabilities.
options.C: cannot exercise the significant influence that proportionate consolidation is designed to reflect.
options.A: holds an interest below the 50% threshold at which proportionate consolidation becomes available.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 77 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.B: Correct. IFRS classifies a joint arrangement by the rights and obligations it confers. A joint venture gives the parties rights to the net assets, which the single-line equity method reflects, whereas proportionate consolidation would imply a claim on each underlying asset that the venturer does not hold. A joint operation, where the parties do have rights to assets and obligations for liabilities, is instead reported by recognising the venturer's own share of each line.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Joint control is more than significant influence, not less, and an associate with mere significant influence also uses the equity method. The reason proportionate consolidation is ruled out is the nature of the rights conferred.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No ownership percentage makes proportionate consolidation available for a joint venture; classification turns on rights and obligations, and an interest carrying control would call for full consolidation instead.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A parent owns 70% of a subsidiary. Relative to reporting that investee under the equity method, full consolidation will most likely result in:

options.C: a lower net profit margin and an unchanged return on equity attributable to the parent.
options.A: a higher net profit margin and a lower return on equity attributable to the parent.
options.B: an unchanged net profit margin and a higher return on equity attributable to the parent.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 78 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Correct. Consolidation grosses up revenue, assets and liabilities by 100% of the subsidiary while net income attributable to the parent and equity attributable to the parent are identical under both treatments. A larger revenue base against the same bottom line lowers the net profit margin, parent-basis ROE is unchanged, and the assets-to-equity leverage ratio rises because the subsidiary's debt now appears on the face of the balance sheet.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The margin moves the other way. The equity method reports the investor's share of the investee's profit with none of its revenue, which is why one-line treatment flatters margins and is a standard reason analysts recast an equity-method investee.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Parent-basis return on equity is the one major ratio that does not move, because neither the numerator nor the denominator changes. What changes is the size and composition of the balance sheet and the income statement.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: An acquirer pays USD 720 million in cash for 80% of a target whose identifiable net assets have a fair value of USD 800 million. The fair value of the 20% non-controlling interest is USD 170 million. Under the full goodwill method, goodwill recognised on the acquisition is closest to:

options.B: USD 80 million.
options.C: USD 90 million.
options.A: USD 100 million.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 79 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 80 million is partial goodwill, USD 720 million less 80% of USD 800 million, which recognises only the parent's share. IFRS lets an acquirer choose either method deal by deal, while US GAAP requires the full goodwill method.
explanations.C: Correct. Full goodwill takes the fair value of the whole entity, being the consideration transferred plus the fair value of the non-controlling interest, less the fair value of the identifiable net assets: USD 720 million plus USD 170 million less USD 800 million. The USD 10 million by which this exceeds partial goodwill is the goodwill attributable to the non-controlling interest.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 100 million grosses the purchase price up to an implied whole-entity value of USD 900 million. That shortcut is a fallback only when the fair value of the non-controlling interest is unobservable; here it is given, and grossing up wrongly extends the parent's control premium to the minority shares.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: An acquirer that measures the non-controlling interest at its fair value rather than at its proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets will, at the acquisition date, most likely report:

options.A: higher total assets and a lower return on equity computed on total equity.
options.B: higher total assets and a higher return on equity computed on total equity.
options.C: unchanged total assets and a lower return on equity computed on total equity.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 80 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Correct. Measuring the non-controlling interest at fair value produces full goodwill, which raises goodwill and total assets, with the offsetting credit raising the non-controlling interest inside total equity by the same amount. Acquisition-date net income is unaffected, so the larger equity base lowers return on total equity, and it also lowers return on assets and the debt-to-equity ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Return on equity falls rather than rises, because the extra goodwill inflates the denominator while leaving earnings alone. Full goodwill makes an acquirer look better capitalised but less profitable on a returns basis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Total assets do change. The additional goodwill recognised under the full method is exactly the excess of the non-controlling interest's fair value over its proportionate share of identifiable net assets, and it is carried as an asset.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A parent recognises an impairment of goodwill arising from an earlier acquisition. In the year the charge is taken, it will most likely:

options.A: reduce cash flow from operations, because the write-down is charged as an operating expense.
options.B: be reversed in a later period if the recoverable amount of the cash-generating unit recovers.
options.C: reduce net income and total assets while leaving cash flow from operations unchanged.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 81 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The charge reduces net income but is added back in arriving at cash flow from operations, so operating cash flow is unaffected; its appearance as an add-back is one way to spot it in the cash flow statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reversal of a goodwill impairment loss is prohibited under both IFRS and US GAAP, in contrast to most other long-lived assets under IFRS, where an impairment may be reversed if the recoverable amount recovers.
explanations.C: Correct. Goodwill impairment is a non-cash charge: it lowers net income, goodwill and equity, but is added back in the indirect-method reconciliation, and because it is generally not deductible it does not change cash taxes either. That cash-flow neutrality is why analysts read the charge mainly as a belated admission that the acquisition price was too high.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Compared with a defined contribution plan, a defined benefit plan is best described as an arrangement in which:

options.A: the employee bears the investment risk and the employer's expense equals the contribution promised for the period.
options.B: the employer bears the investment and actuarial risk and reports the plan's funded status on the balance sheet.
options.C: the obligation is discharged each period, so no asset or liability beyond unpaid contributions can arise.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 82 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. This describes a defined contribution plan, in which the employer's obligation ends with the agreed contribution and the employee carries the investment outcome into retirement.
explanations.B: Correct. A defined benefit promise fixes the future payment, so the employer absorbs the consequences of poor asset returns, longevity, salary growth and discount rate movements, and must report the difference between the obligation and plan assets. The measurement therefore rests on actuarial assumptions that management itself chooses.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Settlement each period with no residual balance is again the defined contribution pattern. A defined benefit plan leaves an obligation extending decades beyond the reporting date.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A company's defined benefit pension plan reports a present value of the defined benefit obligation of EUR 940 million and plan assets with a fair value of EUR 785 million. Under both IFRS and US GAAP, the balance sheet will most likely show:

options.A: a net pension liability of EUR 155 million, the underfunded status of the plan.
options.B: a pension liability of EUR 940 million, with the plan assets presented separately.
options.C: a net pension liability of EUR 155 million, reduced by any unrecognised actuarial losses.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 83 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Correct. The reported amount is the funded status, the obligation less the fair value of plan assets, recognised in full. An overfunded plan gives a net asset instead, subject to a ceiling on the economic benefit recoverable from the surplus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plan assets are held in a separate trust for the benefit of participants and are legally beyond the employer's reach, so they are netted against the obligation rather than shown gross among the employer's own assets.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deferring unrecognised actuarial gains and losses through a corridor was the old smoothing regime; current standards put the full funded status on the balance sheet and push the smoothing into other comprehensive income instead.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Under US GAAP, a company reports the following for its defined benefit plan for the year: current service cost USD 60 million; interest cost on the obligation USD 48 million; expected return on plan assets USD 40 million; prior service cost of USD 30 million granted during the year and amortised over an average remaining service life of 10 years; and an actuarial loss of USD 25 million arising in the year, none of which is amortised in the current period. Pension expense recognised in profit or loss is closest to:

options.B: USD 68 million.
options.C: USD 98 million.
options.A: USD 71 million.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 84 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 68 million omits the USD 3 million amortisation of prior service cost. US GAAP defers the grant to OCI but then feeds it into expense over the remaining service life, so it cannot be left out entirely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 98 million expenses the whole USD 30 million prior service cost immediately, which is the IFRS treatment of past service cost rather than the US GAAP treatment. This difference is one reason pension expense is not comparable across regimes without adjustment.
explanations.A: Correct. US GAAP builds the income statement charge as service cost of USD 60 million plus interest cost of USD 48 million less the expected return of USD 40 million plus amortisation of prior service cost of USD 30 million over ten years, or USD 3 million, giving USD 71 million. The USD 30 million grant and the USD 25 million actuarial loss go to other comprehensive income when they arise and reach profit or loss only through amortisation.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: In a year in which market yields were unchanged, a US GAAP filer raises both the discount rate used to measure its defined benefit obligation and the expected long-term rate of return on plan assets, and lowers its assumed rate of compensation growth. The combined effect of these three changes is most likely to:

options.A: increase reported pension expense while reducing the reported obligation.
options.B: reduce reported pension expense and reduce the reported obligation.
options.C: reduce reported pension expense while increasing the reported obligation.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 85 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. None of the three changes raises expense. The expected return enters the US GAAP charge as a deduction, so increasing it lowers reported pension cost, which is one reason IFRS replaced the expected return with net interest at the discount rate.
explanations.B: Correct. A higher discount rate and a lower salary growth assumption each shrink the present value of the obligation and the current service cost, and a higher expected return on plan assets reduces US GAAP pension expense directly. All three push in the same favourable direction, and moving all of them at once in a year when market yields did not change is a recognised earnings-quality warning sign rather than a neutral re-estimate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The obligation falls rather than rises: discounting future benefits at a higher rate lowers their present value, and assuming slower pay growth lowers the benefits being discounted. The expected return assumption does not touch the obligation at all.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: An analyst is recasting the reported statements of a company with a materially underfunded defined benefit plan. The adjustment most consistent with the economics of the plan is to:

options.C: add the underfunded status to total debt and reclassify the interest component of pension cost as a financing expense.
options.A: remove the whole periodic pension cost from operating expenses and treat the funded status as an operating liability.
options.B: capitalise the current service cost as an intangible asset and exclude the interest component from the income statement.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 86 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Correct. The funded status is a claim on the firm that behaves like borrowing, so leverage and enterprise value measures are more comparable once it is treated as debt. Only the current service cost is genuinely a cost of employing people in the period, so it stays in operating expenses, while the interest on the obligation and the return on plan assets are financing and investing in nature.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Stripping out the entire pension cost also removes the current service cost, which is real compensation earned in the period, and so overstates operating profit. Classifying the funded status as an operating liability additionally understates financial leverage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Service cost is an expense of the period, not an asset, so capitalising it defers compensation already earned. Deleting the interest component altogether, rather than reclassifying it, simply removes a real cost from the income statement.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A company grants part of its employee compensation as equity-settled share options instead of cash. Relative to paying the same total compensation entirely in cash, it will most likely report:

options.B: no compensation expense until the options are exercised, and no change to the share count.
options.C: compensation expense over the vesting period, no operating cash outflow, and dilution of existing shareholders.
options.A: compensation expense equal to the intrinsic value of the options, remeasured at each reporting date.

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 87 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.B: Incorrect. Deferring all recognition to exercise would let a company report compensation-free profits during the very years employees earn the award; the cost is recognised across the vesting period instead.
explanations.C: Correct. Equity-settled options are measured at grant-date fair value and expensed over the vesting period, so reported profit bears the cost, but because nothing is paid the charge is added back as a non-cash item and operating cash flow is higher than for an all-cash payer. The offsetting credit goes to equity, and existing holders are diluted on exercise, which is why comparing companies on cash flow alone rewards heavy option issuers.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Intrinsic value remeasured each period is not the model for equity-settled options, which are fixed at grant-date fair value. Ongoing remeasurement applies to cash-settled, liability-classified awards such as share appreciation rights.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A parent whose presentation currency is the US dollar is determining the functional currency of a newly acquired foreign subsidiary under IFRS. Which fact most likely indicates that the subsidiary's functional currency is the US dollar rather than its local currency?

options.A: The subsidiary keeps its accounting records and files statutory accounts in the local currency
options.B: The subsidiary's selling prices are set by the parent and denominated in US dollars
options.C: The subsidiary's labour and materials are sourced locally and paid for in local currency

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 88 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. The currency in which books are kept or statutory accounts are filed is a bookkeeping and legal-filing matter. Functional currency is determined by the economic substance of the entity's operations, not by the ledger currency.
explanations.B: Correct. The primary indicators are the currency that mainly influences sales prices and the currency of the costs of providing goods and services. Prices set by the parent and denominated in US dollars point to a US dollar functional currency, which means the subsidiary is remeasured using the temporal method.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Locally sourced and locally settled costs are an indicator pointing the other way, toward the local currency being functional and therefore toward the current rate method with a cumulative translation adjustment.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: On 1 November a company whose functional and presentation currency is the US dollar sells goods for FC 500,000, with payment due the following 1 February. The spot rate is USD 0.80 per FC on 1 November and USD 0.75 per FC on 31 December, the company's fiscal year end. The amount recognised for this foreign currency transaction for the year ended 31 December is most likely:

options.C: a loss of USD 25,000, reported in other comprehensive income
options.A: a loss of USD 25,000, reported in net income
options.B: a gain of USD 25,000, reported in net income

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 89 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.C: Incorrect. The amount is right but the location is not. Other comprehensive income is where the cumulative translation adjustment from translating a foreign subsidiary accumulates; a transaction gain or loss on a monetary item held by the reporting entity itself does not go there.
explanations.A: Correct. The receivable is a foreign-currency monetary asset, so it is remeasured at the balance sheet date even though it is unsettled: FC 500,000 x 0.80 = USD 400,000 at inception against FC 500,000 x 0.75 = USD 375,000 at year end, a USD 25,000 loss taken to net income under both IFRS and US GAAP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This inverts the rate move. The foreign currency has weakened against the US dollar, from 0.80 to 0.75, so each FC of the receivable buys fewer dollars and the holder of an FC-denominated asset records a loss.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: Under the current rate method of translating a foreign subsidiary's financial statements, which item is most likely translated at a historical exchange rate?

options.A: Long-term debt denominated in the subsidiary's local currency
options.B: Depreciation expense on the subsidiary's property and equipment
options.C: Common stock issued by the subsidiary at the acquisition date

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 90 | Financial Statement Analysis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Under the current rate method every asset and every liability, monetary or not, is translated at the balance sheet date rate; long-term debt is no exception, which is why the method is named for that rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Income statement items under the current rate method are translated at the average rate for the period. It is the temporal method that translates depreciation at the historical rate of the underlying asset.
explanations.C: Correct. Contributed capital is the exception to the current rate: common stock and additional paid-in capital stay at the rate in effect when the capital was contributed. That mismatch against net assets translated at the current rate is exactly what the cumulative translation adjustment balances.

cfa_l2.subject: Financial Statement Analysis

cfa_l2.stem: A subsidiary is remeasured using the temporal method and carries inventory at historical cost on a FIFO basis. Beginning inventory of FC 200 was acquired when the rate was USD 0.50 per FC, purchases during the year were FC 1,000 at an average rate of USD 0.55 per FC, and ending inventory of FC 300 was acquired when the rate was USD 0.57 per FC. The year-end rate is USD 0.60 per FC. Remeasured cost of goods sold is closest to:

options.C: USD 470
options.A: USD 479
options.B: USD 495

cfa_l2.origin: CFA Level II | Practice item 91 | Financial Statement Analysis
